content: African tick bite fever is an infectious disease caused by a specific type of bacteria. The infection occurs when an individual is bitten by a tick that carries the bacteria. Symptoms typically manifest within two weeks following the tick bite. The initial sign is often a red sore at the site of the bite, which develops a dark crust known as an eschar. If multiple tick bites occur, multiple eschars may be present. As the disease progresses, additional symptoms may include fever, headache, muscle soreness, swollen lymph nodes, and a rash. African tick bite fever is the most frequently reported tick-borne illness among travelers. Travelers to sub-Saharan Africa, parts of the Caribbean, and Oceania (including Australia, New Zealand, Melanesia, Micronesia, and Polynesia) are at risk of contracting African tick bite fever. The risk is heightened for individuals engaging in outdoor activities such as camping, hiking, or game hunting in wooded, brushy, or grassy areas. Ticks carrying the bacteria responsible for this disease are most active between November and April. There are no vaccines available to prevent African tick bite fever. Travelers can reduce their risk of infection by taking the following precautions: 1. Prevent Tick Bites: Be aware of where ticks are commonly found. Ticks inhabit grassy, brushy, or wooded areas and may also be found on animals. Activities such as camping, gardening, or hunting can increase exposure to ticks. Ticks can even be encountered in residential yards or neighborhoods. Use permethrin to treat boots, clothing, and camping gear. Permethrin-treated items remain protective through several washes. Alternatively, purchase pre-treated clothing and gear. Apply insect repellents containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535, oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE), para-menthane-diol (PMD), or 2-undecanone. Always follow product instructions, and avoid using products containing OLE or PMD on children under three years old. 2. Avoid Contact with Ticks: Steer clear of wooded and brushy areas with tall grass and leaf litter. Walk in the center of trails to minimize exposure. 3. Find and Remove Ticks: Inspect clothing for ticks after spending time outdoors. Ticks can be carried into the home on clothing and should be removed promptly. Dry clothes in a dryer on high heat for 10 minutes to kill ticks on dry clothing. If clothes are damp, additional drying time may be required. If washing is necessary, use hot water, as cold or medium-temperature water will not kill ticks. Examine gear and pets for ticks. Ticks can hitch a ride on clothing, pets, or gear and later attach to humans. Carefully inspect pets, coats, and backpacks. Shower soon after returning indoors. Showering within two hours of being outdoors has been shown to reduce the risk of tick-borne diseases. Showering can help wash off unattached ticks and provides an opportunity to perform a thorough tick check. Conduct a full-body tick check using a hand-held or full-length mirror to inspect all parts of the body. Pay special attention to areas such as: Under the arms In and around the ears Inside the belly button Back of the knees In and around the hair Between the legs Around the waist If a tick is found attached to the skin, it should be removed as soon as possible.
